title: Fidelity and Fracture
text:
A translator who approaches a novel as a mere transfer of information soon discovers that the text resists such reduction. Each sentence carries a cadence, a historical undertone, and a set of allusions that do not map neatly onto the target language. The translator must therefore navigate between literal accuracy and the preservation of tone. Many decisions that appear trivial, such as the choice of a single verb, can alter the emotional register of an entire chapter.

Some readers consider the translator a faithful servant, invisible and self-effacing. Others, however, regard the translator as a co-author whose interpretive choices shape how a work is received across cultures. Neither view is wholly satisfactory, for the translator is neither a passive conduit nor an unrestrained rewriter. Rather, the ideal lies in a disciplined sensitivity that honors the source while acknowledging the inevitability of loss.

options: As a faithful servant who remains invisible
As a famous novelist in their own right
As a publisher who selects the books

questions.text: What does the author imply about a translator who rewrites the text freely?
options: They risk overstepping the role of a disciplined interpreter
They always produce a more accurate version
They are praised by all readers equally
They avoid making any decisions about tone

questions.text: What is the author's position on the loss that occurs in translation?
options: It is inevitable and must be acknowledged
It can be eliminated by a careful enough translator
It matters only to literary critics
It occurs mainly because of publishers' demands

paragraph_translations: Un traductor que aborda una novela como una simple transferencia de información pronto descubre que el texto se resiste a tal reducción. Cada frase lleva una cadencia, un trasfondo histórico y un conjunto de alusiones que no se corresponden con facilidad con la lengua meta. Por ello, el traductor debe moverse entre la exactitud literal y la preservación del tono. Muchas decisiones que parecen triviales, como la elección de un solo verbo, pueden alterar el registro emocional de un capítulo entero.

Algunos lectores consideran al traductor un servidor fiel, invisible y discreto. Otros, en cambio, lo ven como un coautor cuyas decisiones interpretativas moldean cómo se recibe una obra en distintas culturas. Ninguna de las dos visiones es del todo satisfactoria, pues el traductor no es un conducto pasivo ni un reescritor sin freno. Más bien, el ideal reside en una sensibilidad disciplinada que honra el original y reconoce la inevitabilidad de la pérdida.
